Pilferage of Gas From L.P.G. Cylinders 
†541. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA : Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the increasing 
incidents of pilferage of gas from LPG cylinders; 
(b) if so, whether Government have taken any action for checking such 
incidents; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Pilferage of Gas From LPG Cylinders 
(a) to (c) The Government is aware of the incidents of pilferage of gas 
from liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) cylinders. Following measures are being 
taken to prevent pilferage of LPG from cylinders :— 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
2 

[29 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(i) Liquefied Petroleum Gas (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) 
Order, 2000 under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 has been promulgated. 
As per this Order, pilfering product from cylinder/supply of partially used 
cylinder to LPG consumer by the distributors of Public Sector Oil Marketing 
Companies (OMCs) as well as Parallel Marketeers has been prohibited. 
 
(ii) State Governments are also empowered to take action against the 
erring distributors under the provisions of the above Order. 
 
(iii) Marketing Discipline Guidelines  (MDG) for LPG distributors of 
OMCs have been laid down by the Government in April, 2001. According to 
these guidelines, in case of establishment of any complaint of pilferage/supply 
of partially used cylinders to customer, a fine of Rs. 20,000 plus the price of 
LPG pilfered/supplied short at commercial rate for 1st offence, Rs. 50,000 plus 
the price of LPG pilfered/supplied short at commercial rate for 2nd offence, 
and termination for 3rd offence by the distributor is imposed. 
 
(iv) LPG distributors of OMCs are under strict instructions to supply 
the cylinders of right quantity and quality to their customers. The officials of 
OMCs carry out random checks at distributor's godown, delivery point as 
well as enroute to ensure that no pilferage takes place. On the establishment 
of any complaint of pilferage or supply of partially used cylinder to customer, 
action against the erring distributor is taken in terms of MDG and/or 
Distributorship Agreement. 
 
OMCs have reported 41 established cases of pilferage/supply of 
partially used cylinders to customers against their distributors during the year 
2002-2003 as against 37 cases during the year 2001-2002.

*545. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ : Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government have received any proposal for utilization of 
sea water by the process of Reverse Osmosis Plant for supplying water to

SETHI): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement  
Utilization of Sea Water 
(a) No proposal for utilization of sea water by Reverse Osmosis plant 
process for supplying water to Kutch region in Gujarat has been received by 
the Ministry of Water Resources. 
(b) and (c) Do not arise. 
SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ : Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to know 
from the hon. Minister, looking at the acute shortage of water in Kutch area 
of Gujarat, which is surrounded by sea and salty desert, will the Government 
at least agreed to consider any such process for utilization of sea water, as it 
is being utilised by United Arab Emirates, Qatar and other countries? 
SHRI ARJUN CHARAN SETHI: Sir, the reply to the question asked by 
my hon. friend is: 'No proposal for utilization of sea water by Reverse Osmosis 
Plant process for supplying water to Kuch region in Gujarat has been received 
by the Ministry of Water Resources'. And, reply to 'b' and 'c' is: 'Do not arise'. 
Sir, as far as the question asked by the hon. Member in regard to the projects 
to utilise the sea water is concerned, in the year 1998, power had been 
delegated to the States to plan, execute and maintain individual water supply 
schemes. So, now it is not under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Water 
Resources or the Government of India. It is upto the States; they are to plan, 
execute and maintain individual projects, which they deem fit under the 
scheme. 
SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Availability of water must be considered 
by the Government of India. And, when there is no other source in the Kutch 
16 

[29 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
area, which is surrounded by sea and desert, what is the harm, what is the difficulty

being utilised in other countries of the world?

reported that about 150 Reverse Osmosis Plants have been commissioned throughout 
the country. Out of these 150 plants, 77 are functioning. In Gujarat, out of the 12 
plants installed, one plant is now functioning. It is very costly. That is why it becomes 
very difficult for the State Governments to maintain it.

a similar proposal for utilisation of sea water for regular water supply has been 
received from the Government of Tamil Nadu. If there is any proposal, what is the

SHRI ARJUN CHARAN SETHI: Sir, as I have already stated, this power has 
been delegated to the State Governments in the year 1998. Therefore, it is up to the 
State Governments. They can plan, execute and maintain the project.

AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to refer to the answer to Unstarred

higher private initiative and greater integration with the world economy, 
reducing the level of poverty and facilitating greater investment; 
(b) the targets set out for 2003-2004 in these sectors; 
(c) whether the war in Iraq will affect the targets set out;

JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (e) A statement is placed on the table of the

Statement 
Impact of Iraq war on economy (a) As per available 
information share of the private sector in the total Gross Domestic Product 
(GDP) increased from 74.1 per cent in 1993-94 to 76.0 per cent in 2001-02. 
During the same period, the share of private sector 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2003] 
investment in total investment increased from 61.2 per cent to 71.8 per cent. 
The share of total exports of goods and services in GDP, which is a measure 
of integration with the world economy, increased from 7.1 per cent in 1990-91 
to 13.3 per cent in 2001-02. There has also been significant increase in Foreign 
Investment that increased from US $ 103 million in 1990-91 to US $ 59.25 
million in 2001-02. The poverty ratio declined by nearly 10 percentage point 
in the five year period following 1993-94 to reach 26.1 per cent in 1999-2000. 
(b) The growth rates are not set on an annual basis. The Tenth Plan 
(2002—07) has envisaged the share of private investment in total investment 
at 70 per cent and the share of exports and imports in GDP at 14.24 per cent 
and 17.71 per cent respectively. It has set a target of reduction of poverty by 
5 percentage points by 2007. The panch priorities of the Union Budget 2003-04, 
which include, inter alia, poverty eradication, infrastructure development and 
accelerating reform process, are expected to create a conducive environment 
for accelerating private investment ensuring greater integration with world 
economy and consequently result in the reduction of poverty. 
(c) to (e) The Government constantly reviews the situation arising out 
of the Iraq War and appropriate steps are taken in accordance with national 
interests and policy objectives. Measures were taken to insulate the economy 
from volatility in international crude oil prices. In the post-war scenario, it is 
our expectation Iraq will offer greater opportunities for trade and commerce 
with that country.

styled as Iraq War because the content of the question has only tangential 
reference to the Iraq War.

*550. SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleaded to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a former Water Resources Minister, Shri K. L. 
Rao had got the proposal of linking of Ganga River with Southern rivers 
examined; 
(b) if so, the details and conclusions of study undertaken at that time; and 
(c) the reasons for abandoning that scheme at that time? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN SETHI) 
: (a) The then Central Water and Power Commission prepared a note on the 
National Water Grid in 1972 and suggested three possible alignments for the 
Ganga-Cauvery links. Dr. K. L. Rao further studied the note of the Central Water 
and Power Commission and advocated one of the alignments for the Ganga-
Cauvery link along with a few other links including the Ganga-Brahmaputra link. 
(b) The Ganga-Cauvery link essentially envisaged withdrawal of 1680 cumec 
of the flood flows of the Ganga near Patna for about 150 days in a year and 
pumping about 1400 cumec of this water over a head of 549 metres for transfer 
to the Peninsular region and utilising the remaining 280 cumec in Ganga basin 
itself. The proposal envisaged utilisation of 2.59 Million hectare metre of Ganga 
water to bring under irrigation an additional area of 4 Million hectare. 
(c)The Ganga-Cauvery link as proposed by Dr. K. L. Rao was examined 
by Central Water Commission and found to be grossly underestimated. Besides

power for lifting water. The proposal was, therefore, given up.

reserves in their respective States; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN SETHI): 
(a) and (b) Ministry of Environment Forests launched a scheme on Conservation and 
Management of Water Reserves viz. Wetlands, Mangroves and Coral Reefs during 
1987. The scheme is continuing in Tenth Five year Plan. The Ministry of Environment and 
Forests have identified 24 wetland areas in the country for conservation and 
management till date. The list of such areas is given in the enclosed statement. (See 
below) Objectives of the scheme cover identification of priority areas for conservation 
and management and prepare policy guidelines for implementation of management 
action plans for these identified areas. Activities under these action plans include 
survey and demarcation, protection, forestation, natural regeneration, restoration, 
catchment area treatment, pollution control, weed control, wild life conservation, 
fisheries development, environmental education etc. 
In addition, for conservation of water resources in the country, a large number 
of major and medium reservoirs providing 177 Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) of storage 
capacity have been created. Another 207.77 BCM of storage is likely to be created 
through ongoing and proposed projects. 
(c) and (d) Management Action Plans for the identified wetlands, mangroves 
and coral reefs are implemented by the respective State Governments/ Union territories. To 
monitor progress of implementation of these Management Action Plans, State level 
Steering Committees have been constituted in all the concerned States. 
The National Water policy—2002, adopted by the National Water Resources 
Council, also emphasizes on conservation of water. The policy provides that 
efficiency of utilisation in all the diverse uses of water should be optimised and an 
awareness of water as a scarce resource should be fostered. The policy further states 
that the resources should be conserved and the availability augmented by 
maximising retention eliminating pollution and minimising losses. The National 
Water Policy has been sent to all the State Governments/Union Territories for 
implementation. The policy also directs that each State shall formulate its own State Water 
Policy backed with an operational

till a decision is taken on their licence applications by RBI. In respect of the 
Banks which are likely to comply with the licence norms in the near future, RBI 
has considered it advisable to give time to do the needful. Apart from these, 
there are 58 Co-operative Societies (54 in Kerala, 1 in Assam and 3 in Manipur) 
carrying on banking business without licence from RBI, on the basis of 
registration given by Registrar of Co-operative Societies (RCS) of the respective 
States. In addition, there are entitites, one in Orissa and the other one in Uttar 
Pradesh, carrying on banking business unauthorisedly. 
RBI has taken up the cases of unlicensed banks with the respective State 
Governments. Some unlicensed Urban Co-operative Banks in Kerala have filed 
writ petition in the High Court of Kerala to quash the circular issued by the 
Registrar of Co-operative Societies of Kerala on 23rd January, 2003 to all Joint 
Registrar of Co-operative So cieties in the Districts and registered unlicensed 
Co-operative Urban banks to stop any violation of Banking regulation Act and 
to change their constitution to Urban Co-operative Societies by making necessary 
changes in their by-laws within two months. The Court issued an interim direction 
on 24th March, 2003 restraining the State of Kerala from taking any coercive 
steps for non-compliance of the circular dated 23rd January, 2003.

COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANAND RAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) 
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had announced the mid-term review of monetary 
and credit policy for the year 2002-03 on October 29,2002. In this, the RBI has 
reviewed the macroeconomic developments and indicated that the stance of 
monetary policy in the remaining part of the year will continue to be one of 
providing adequate liquidity to meet credit growth and support investment 
demand in the economy and imparting greater flexibility to the interest rate

4.75 per cent. Other policy measures announced in the mid-term review include, 
inter-alia, partial liberalisation of interest rates on rupee export credit,

credit delivery. The findings of the review and changes in credit policy

Statement-II 
Measures taken to increase the flow of Credit to SSI Sector 
1. Banks to provide working capital to SSI sector on the basis of 
minimum of 20% of projected turnover. The upper ceilings were 
gradually enhanced from Rs. 2 crore to Rs, 4 crore in Union 
Budget 1998-99 and from Rs. 4 crore to Rs 5 crore (Union Budget 
1999-2000). 
2. Raising of the Composite loan limit from Rs. 10 lakhs to Rs. 25 
lakhs. 
3. Raising the limit of Projects to Rs. 50 lakhs for providing 
assistance under National Equity Fund Scheme. 
4. Increase in the borrowal limit for collateral free loan to tiny sector 
from Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 5 lakhs. The RBI in its Credit Policy 2002-
03 has announced that the banks may on the basis of good track 
record of units, and their financial position, further increase the 
limit of dispensing with collateral requirement for loans from Rs. 5 
lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs. 
5. Launching of Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Small Industries 
to cover collateral-free and third party guarantee free loans of 
commercial banks to SSI sector including IT and software sector, 
upto a limit of Rs. 10 lakhs (since enhanced to Rs. 25 lakh). A 
separate Trust viz. ,Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small 
Industries have been jointly set up by SIDBI and Government of 
India for the purpose and the Scheme is already operational since 
August 2000. 
6. Introduction of Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for 
Technology Upgradation of SSIs (CLCSS) in the select 
products/sub-sectors. 
7. The individual credit limit to artisans, village and cottage 
industries for reckoning under advance to weaker sections is 
increased from Rs. 25,000/- to Rs. 50,000/-. 
8. Earmarking of 30% of the investment under NEF for the tiny 
sector. 
Loans for unemployed graduates in Uttaranchal 
4117. SHRI HARISH RAWAT : Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state : 
(a)   whether Government are aware of the problems faced by the 
unemployed graduates in getting loans from the banks in Uttaranchal; 
116 

[29 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to relax such rules for the 
unemployed from backward and snow bound areas and other weaker sections in 
the State as special case; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VTTHOBA ADSUL): (a) State Bank 
of India (SBI), the Convenor of State Level Bankers Committee (SLBC) for the 
State of Uttaranchal has reported that no instance of any specific problems 
faced by the unemployed graduates in getting loans from the banks in Uttaranchal 
has come to their notice. 
(b) and (c) Government of India have launched a subsidy linked scheme 
on 2-10-1993 viz. the Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) for creating self 
employment opportunities for the educated unemployed youth including 
graduates, by setting up micro enterprises in business, industry and service 
sector. The objective of the scheme is to provide self-employment opportunities 
to educated unemployed youth. In order to mitigate the problems being faced by 
the borrowers and also to expand the coverage and scope of the scheme some 
amendments have been made with effect from 22-1-1999. The major amendments 
are: 
(i)Age: The maximum age limit raised from 35 to 45 years for SC/ST, Ex-
servicemen/physi;ally handicapped & women candidates. 
(ii) Educational Qualifications: Relaxed from Matric/ITI to class VIII 
passed. 
(iii) Activities covered: The range of activities covered has been expanded 
to include agriculture and allied activities but excluding direct 
agricultural operations like raising crop, purchase of manure etc. 
(iv) Family Income: Theeligjbility limit hasbeen increased from Rs. 24,000/-
to Rs. 40,000/- per annum. 
These parameters/guidelines for PMRY have been further relaxed in 
case of North Eastern States. 
(j) Age Limit: Raised from 35 years to 40 years for General Candidates 
plus 10 years for SC/ST and Women candidates. 
(ii) Subsidy : @ 15%, Maximum subsidy increased from Rs. 7,500/-
toRs. 15000/-. 
(iii) Margin Money: From 5% to 12.5% of the project cost (against fixed 
5% earlier) so as to make the subsidy and margin contribution at 20% of 
the project cost. 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2003] 
(iv) Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana: (SGSY) scheme is a major poverty 
linked credit programme for the needs of the Below Poverty Line (BPL) 
borrower and aims at establishing a large number of micro enterprises in the 
rural areas of the country. The objective of the SGSY is to bring the assisted 
poor families (Swarozgaries) above the poverty line by ensuring sustained 
level of income over a period of time. This objective is to be achieved by inter-
alia, organizing rural poor into Self Help Groups (SHGs) through the process of 
social mobilization, training, capacity building and provision of income 
generating assets. 
(v) Eligibility: Rural poor such as the landless labour, small and marginal farmers, 
those with marginal land, rural artisans and educated unemployed 
enlisted in the BPL list up to an age limit of 60 years. 
(vi) Reservation: 50% for SC/ST, 40% for women and 3% for handicapped, 50% of 
Self-Help Groups (SHGs). Under the scheme, generally a Self Help Group 
consists of 10—20 persons. However, a relaxation in these criteria has been 
allowed by RBI that in difficult areas like deserts, hills and areas with scattered 
and sparse population the number of persons in the group may vary from 5—
20. Generally all members of the group should belong to families below the 
poverty line (BPL). Further, relaxation provided that, if necessary, a 
maximum of 20% and in exceptional cases, where essentially required, upto a 
maximum of 30% of the members in a group may be taken from families 
marginally above the poverty line living continuously with BPL families and if 
they are acceptable to the BPL members of the group.

Research on Utilisation of Rain Water 
4161. SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: 
SHRIMATI CHANDRA KALA PANDEY : 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to promote the research on utilization of 
unutilized rain water to tackle the problems of water crisis in various parts of the country; 
and 
(b) if so, the details thereof, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) The National Water Policy 
envisages need for intensifying research efforts in the areas of water harvesting and 
ground water recharge, water conservation, better water management practices and 
improvements in operational technology among others. The Government is also 
promoting rain water harvesting technology for utiliza' ion of rain water. Percolation 
tanks, check dams, gabion structures, dug well rec structure, recharge shafts, rooftop rain 
water collection are some of the means of rain water harvesting. Various innovations 
in water conservation by augmentation, efficient utilisation and water quality 
preservation have been 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2003] 
developed and are being practiced in the country. Mass awareness campaign is being 
run to bring awareness for water as a scarce resource and need for water conservation 
and its efficient utilisation through peoples' participation. 
Central Ground Water Board has taken up a Central Sector Scheme on ' Studies 
of Recharge to Ground Water' on pilot basis to appraise the applicability of these 
innovations. Under this, 174 schemes have been taken up in various parts of the 
country during Ninth Five Year Plan. Under the Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme, Ministry of Rural Development is also providing technical and 
financial assistance to the State Governments and other implementing agencies 
for rain water harvesting through Water Management Programme, artificial recharge of 
ground water and rooftop rain water harvesting. 
Accordingly, several State Governments have taken up the steps to preserve 
traditional water sources such as ponds, canals and rivers to supply drinking water in 
rural as well as urban areas. Government of Madhya Pradesh has launched Pani Roko 
Abhiyan and Government of Andhra Pradesh has started implementation of Neeru-
Meeru (water and you) programme for water conservation. Government of Rajasthan 
has taken up the preservation of their traditional sources of water. Government of 
Maharashtra has started construction of Budkis, deepening and repairs of existing 
wells and other water sources. Government of Gujarat has also started rejuvenation of 
existing water sources.

year. The CGWB has also undertaken a project for salinity ingress and ground water

Master Plans for Conservation of water 
†4170. SHRI MOTILAL VORA : Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any master plans have been prepared for utilizing the traditional 
water sources; 
(b) if so, the States in which master plans have been prepared so far 
alongwith the details thereof; 
(c) by when the master plans would be prepared for rest of the States; and 
(d) by when the implementation on water conservation would be started? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (d) water being a State subject, water 
resources schemes, including master plans, are formulated, planned, executed and 
funded by the respective State Governments. Master Plans are prepared taking into 
consideration the availability of water resources and needs of the areas for which the 
Master Plan is prepared. 
Conventional methods of rain water harvesting, construction of dams and 
minor tanks, restoration of old tanks, watershed management etc., are being practised in 
the country. Central Ground Water Board under Ministry of Water Resources has 
prepared a 'Master Plan for Artificial Recharge to Ground Water' which envisages recharge 
of 36453 Million Cubic Metre volume of water through 2.25 lakh artificial recharge 
structures in rural areas like percolation tanks, check dams, sub-surface dykes, 
gully plugs, gabion structures, nala bunds, contour bunds, recharge shafts etc. In 
addition to this roof-top rainwater harvesting structures in urban areas is proposed 
through 37 lakh structures. The estimated cost of this Master Plan covering all States 
and Union Territories is around Rs. 24,500 crore. 
Water conservation by roof-top rainwater harvesting, selective lining in the 
conveyance systems, minimising losses, modernisation and rehabilitation of existing 
systems and sprinkler and drip irrigation techniques are also being adopted.

Features of Paleo Water 
4173. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY : Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the National Geophysical Research Institute (NGRI) has 
conducted any survey on the oldest water sources in India; 
(b) if so, whether any such survey has been conducted in Hyderabad, 
Andhra Pradesh; 
(c) if so, whether the age of Paleo Water has been ascertained; and 
(d) the characteristics features of such water? 
THE MINISTER OFSTAIEINTHEMINISTRYCF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. The National Geophysical 
Research Institute (NGRI) has carried out survey of ground water resources of 
Neyveli Ground Water Basin, Pondicherry and its environs and Karaikal and 
Thanjavur Deep Aquifers, where Paleo waters are found. The Paleo water age of 
Neyveli Ground Water Basin is 32,000 years old and in the case of other two areas it 
is more than 20,000 years old. 
(b) The NGRI has carried out deep ground water studies in Hyderabad 
Urban Conglomerate covering adjoining districts. 
(c) The deep ground water studies indicated maximum age of 10000 years at 
Dollar Hills in Mehdipatnam, Hyderabad. 
(d) The groundwater is collected from a well having fracture depth at 300 feet 
and the well depth of 450 feet. The chloride content of water is 100 mg/1.

 SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Need to enforce Code of Professional Ethics in Medical Practice in the 
country 
DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa): Sir, my Special Mention concerns the whole 
country. Medical profession is regarded as the noblest of professions. Medical 
fraternity has commanded respect, all over the world, all through ages. 
Though the science itself passes through a continuous process of experiments 
resulting in changes, and yesterday's treatments are regarded outdated today, 
yet, the society had never lost faith either in the medical science or its 
practitioners. As patients regard physicians and surgeons as saviours, they 
repose absolute trust in them while struggling to live. Sir, in recent times, 
however, unethical practices have invaded medical profession. Most 
advanced hospitals with latest medical equipments are being established in 
bigger cities, chiefly with commercial motive. Affluent patients are lured into 
such institutions for safer treatment at heavy costs. But results 
179 

[29 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
are not always necessarily up to the expectation. In Government hospital 
compounds, touts are engaged to lure away patients to private clinics. 
Sophisticated machines are shown as 'out-of-order' in the Government 
hospitals forcing patients to get examined outside. Medicine dealers 
representing big companies prevail upon doctors to prescribe their brands of 
medicine. Spurious drugs are seen flooding medicine shops. Human organs 
are removed from bodies of unsuspecting patients for sale. Even new-born 
babies can be sold for heavy amounts. Surprisingly enough, persons without 
medical education or degree can claim to be qualified doctors in some private 
clinics. Health being a State subject, many State Governments find no money 
to supply most essential elementary necessities to the Primary Health Centres. 
Abysmal conditions in health services need adequate attention for remedy. 
While improving health service, the Government should also try to prevent 
unethical practices in the name of medical practices.

Mention.

Demand for provision of shelter for homeless in the country 
SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU (Pondicherry): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, While the common people treat the homeless with indifference, 
they are also deprived of all their rights from politicians to town planners, the 
police and the municipal bodies. An analysis of the records of Delhi Police 
reveals that the number of unidentified dead bodies has been increasing in the 
city. Lack of space and non-availability of health and medical care seems to 
have led a number of homeless people in the streets of Delhi to death. The 
records of Delhi Police also provide a horrifying figure of 3,040 unidentified 
dead bodies, found in the year 2002; 2,407 dead bodies found in the year 
2001; and 2,348 dead bodies found in the year 2000. These deaths may or 
may not have been natural deaths. But nobody claimed those bodies. This 
proves that they were homeless. The obvious reason for increasing number of 
such deaths of the people living in the streets of Delhi could be, the absence 
of adequate number of shelters for the homeless, and complete disregard of 
their lives in the city. The number of homeless people is increasing day by 
day. There is an urgent need to examine the problems of homeless people. 
The Government should divert its attention to their problem and should make a 
plan to solve their problems. The birds have nest, the tigers have caves, but 
there are no shelters for old and disabled ones. To have a shelter is the right 
of every individual. The Government should pay attention to the rights of 
homeless. The Government should frame rules and regulations to save the 
homeless. Thank you.

Need to ban sale of adulterated and synthetic milk in the country 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Madam, since 
adulteration of milk is on the rise, eating milk products and drinking milk has 
become a matter of concern, and it has become very difficult to distinguish 
between pure milk and adulterated milk. Not only adulterated milk, but even 
synthetic milk in packets, is being sold at doorsteps, with attractive subsidies 
and free gifts to dodge women. Consumption of this milk harms the liver and 
lungs of infants directly and creates digestive problems. Sellers are offering 
free ghee, panneer to those customers who buy milk for one month. It is not 
only taking place in the metropolitan cities, but is also spreading rapidly to 
other small towns and cities. The spurious milk is also entering cities directly 
as pure milk. I have received several complaints about spurious synthetic milk 
being supplied at subsidised rates with attractive gifts during the last few 
weeks. The genuine full cream contains 60 per cent fat. It is available for Rs. 
^7 per litre. These packets can be preserved for two days at 8 degrees. These 
details are printed on the packets. The adulterated packets do not have such 
details printed.   But housewives just see the* brand name and buy the 
product. 
Hence, I request the Government to work in coordination with the 
State Governments, in stopping this menace in the country. Otherwise, this 
adulterated and synthetic milk will create a lot of health hazards in the country. 
I also request that sale of synthetic milk should be banned in our country. 
Need to include Cheraideo in World Heritage sites 
SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN (Assam): Madam, the Archaeological 
Survey of India conducted excavation work at Cheraideo site, in Sibsagar 
District of Assam.    After excavation of Maidaam No.  2, the royal burial 
184 

                    RAJYA SABHA                          [29 April, 2003] 
mound, the Archaeological Survey of India discovered an octagonal burial 
chamber, the remains of human beings and some associated, objects. In reply 
to an Unstarred Question No. 3366, dated 221"1 April, Shri Jagmohan, the hon. 
Minister of Tourism -and Culture, had informed the Members of this House that 
the Archaeological Survey of India has decided to undertake, at the burial 
ground, namely, Maidaam No. 2, at Cheraideo, the work of closing the hole 
that was dug during the British period, to conserve the exposed underground 
burial chamber and make it accessible to the visitors, and also to clean, 
preserve and study the interred human body remains, and the other 
associated objects discovered during the excavation of the monument. He 
further replied that the exposed octagonal wall running round the mound had 
already been conserved. 
Madam, Cheraideo was the first capital of.Ahom Kingdom which 
lasted for six hundred years, from 1227 A.D. up to 1826 A.D. Cheraideo was 
the burial place of Ahom Kings, where more than 32 kings were buried. 
Hence, 32 Maidaams or burial mounds are there. The mortal remains of the 
Kings, along with their valuables, were buried after building structures, over 
which the mound was built. So, these are very important from the historical 
point of view. The pucca royal palaces and other religious monuments of the 
kingdom are also located at Gargaon and Sibsagar, which are a few miles 
away from Cheraideo. So, it is, .undoubtedly a historical site. Therefore, Sir, 
through you, I urge upon the Ministry to declare Cheraideo a World Heritage 
site and make it a good tourist site in the North-Eastern Region of our country.

 SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Madam Deputy 
Chairman, education is a critical input for investment in human capital. As 
against the goal of 6 per cent of the GDP, the total expenditure on education in 
India is currently 4 per cent. Despite all round efforts to make education a 
viable input in economic development, the situation is far from satisfactory. This 
is not to say that education is not capable of meeting the challenges, but the 
state of the art is such that the perceived objectives are difficult to achieve due 
to illiteracy among majority of the people of our country. Plan expenditure on 
education has increased rapidly since the First Five Year Plan.  
Literacy, the basis of all education, is as essential to survival and 
development in modern society as food is to the survival and development of 
the human body. Literacy must be considered the minimum right and 
requirement of every Indian citizen. 
Madam, the educational development in India, however, is 
characterised by glaring disparities. The educationally developed regions 
continued to march forward with a rapid rate, leaving behind the lagging 
regions. This challenge should be met by forward-looking policies of reducing 
regional disparities. 
A high priority has been accorded to this sector in the Tenth Five 
Year Plan. The Parliament had enacted an Act for achieving the goal of 
"Education for All by making elementary education free and compulsory for all 
children in the age group of 6-14 years. India's education system has 
expanded exponentially over the past five decades, but its current 
achievements are grossly inadequate. The net enrolment rate in primary 
schools is around 77 per cent and in secondary schools it is around 60 per 
cent. Literacy among males is nearly 50 per cent higher than females and it is 
about 50 per cent higher in urban areas, as compared to the rural areas. 
Literacy rates range from as high as 100 per cent in some districts of Kerala to 
below 30 per cent in some parts of Madhya Pradesh. These differential rates 
of progress leave approximately 300 million illiterate adults in the country. 
The drop-out rate was 40 per cent at the primary level and 55 per 
cent at the upper primary level in 1999-2000. Out of approximately 200 
million children in the age group of 6 to 14 years, only 120 million are in the 
schools and net attendance in the primary level is only 66 per cent of the 
enrolment.  
189 

[29 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Madam, unless something is done drastically to reduce drop-out 
rates, by the year 2016, there will be approximately 500 million people in the 
country, with less than five years of schooling and another 300 million that will 
not have completed high schools. High drop-out rates in rural areas is due to 
lack of infrastructure. Most of the schools have no class-rooms. Most of the 
schools in rural areas run under the trees and no basic amenities like drinking 
water, toilet facilities -are available. A tremendous expansion of schools and 
class-rooms will be required with basic amenities to school children like 
drinking water and toilet facility to support a quantitative and qualitative 
improvement in the country's school system. 
An important role of education is to foster in each child the attributes 
and values of a responsible, capable, active and healthy member of the family 
and the society. The rigidity of curriculum, testing and teaching methods need 
to be relaxed so that innovative method and new models of education can be 
evolved, tested and perfected. 
Madam, for the development of the country, in general, and the 
individual in particular, the education is the basic need. It is the only way to 
help our next generation in competing with other developed countries. 
Effective measures are to be taken to ensure that the constitutional mandate of 
the free and compulsory education for all the children in the age group of 6 to 
14 years becomes reality. We should make sure that all the Government 
policies and programmes should be implemented more effectively.   Thank 
you.

have gone. There is a gestation period in the Indian economy. What has 
happened in 2002-03 and what is happening in 2003-04 are the outcome of 
the investment decisions taken during the last years of the Ninth Five Year 
Plan. Therefore, if we can take certain corrective measures right now, 
perhaps, we can salvage the situation. Here my first suggestion to the 
Government is that you really prioritise. One good scheme is coming up and I 
welcome it, and I congratulate the Prime Minister for taking the initiative for 
having high quality roads. If we can have high quality roads criss-crossing the 
whole country and maintain them, it will have a tremendous impact on our 
economy. But, after making a beginning, if it is half done, or, if it is incomplete, 
or, if it is not being done properly because of lack of resources, whatever 
investment you are making, that will go waste. It is accepted by the Planning 
Commission Document itself that there are a lot of unutilised capacity. Each 
and every section should have been analysed and examined. Perhaps, this -is 
one of the reasons why the Planning Commission Document points out that it 
is not necessary to go through the normal conventional method that eight per 
cent GDP growth rate would be required for 32.62 per cent of investment as 
percentage of GDP. It means that the incremental capital and output ratio is 
around 3.5-4 per cent. If you can utilise the untapped capacity, the unutilised 
capacity, which has been 
218 

RAJYA SABHA                         [29 April, 2003] 
created by investment of the surpluses of the society, it will give you dividend 
in the remaining 2-3 years. In-between you can really prioritise. One hundred 
things cannot be prioritised. When you want to build the infrastructure, the 
main problems come from the power sector. During the Eighth Plan--I share 
the responsibility because we were in charge of implementing the Eighth Plan-
we could not create the additional capacity which was required to be created 
during the Eighth Plan period. In the Ninth Plan it was practically directionless, 
not only in the power sector, but also in every infrastructure sector, because in 
the entire Plan period notionally the Budgetary allocations were not spent, 
both in the Central Plan sector and in the State Plan sector. As a 
consequence, though in the GDP growth scenario we reached around seven 
per cent during the terminal years of the Eighth Plan, we could not retain it 
and, ultimately, we landed in a modest growth rate of 5.6 per cent. Sir, I have 
no objection if the Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission starts his 
observation - I quote two lines from his observations -- by saying, "the Tenth 
Five Year Plan makes the return of visionary planning to India after a long 
interregnum of cautious optimism." Surely, there was a long interregnum of the 
cautions optimism. We ourselves adopted the philosophy of cautious 
optimism. That is why, at the beginning of the Eighth Plan, which we 
presented, I did not fix the higher target, keeping in view the environmental 
situation, both domestically and internationally, we fixed the growth target at 
5.6 per cent. But, I am happy to inform you, Sir, which this Plan document 
itself points out, that the Eighth Plan target, the GDP target, was originally 
fixed at 5.6 per cent, but we ended up with 6.68 per cent. 
This cautious optimism had paid dividend not only in the Eighth Plan, 
but even in the Seventh Plan, when the targeted growth was 5.0 per cent and 
we ended up with 6.02 per cent. In the Sixth Plan, the targeted growth rate 
was 5.2 per cent and it ended up with 5.4 per cent in real terms. Therefore, we 
must have mission, we must think big. But, it cannot be totally cut-off from the 
reality and the ground reality, today, is that tax GDP is coming down, the 
expenditure GDP is going up. The States and the Centre are to borrow from 
the market at a high rate of interest to meet the normal consumption 
expenditure and still we are tinkering. Several times, it has been debated on 
the floor of this House and the other House that we always raise accusing 
finger towards subsidies. I do agree that our economy cannot bear the burden 
of 15 to 16 per cent of GDP .as subsidies. But, merely expressing our concern 
is not enough.   We shall have to take 
219 

[29 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
concrete steps to reduce it. We have suggested repeatedly, let there be an 
informal discussion; let a paper be brought out. Let all concerned politico! 
parties, industrialists and trade unions be fully involved and identify the areas 
where subsidies are absolutely necessary and where the subsidies could be 
cut. If it could be brought down from 15 or 16 per cent to. 9 or 10 per cent, lot 
of savings would be there. 
Are we really serious in respect of the borrowings? This is a question, 
which is coming to my mind. Unless we tackle the problem of the revenue 
deficit, and, if the revenue deficit runs three to three and a half per cent by 
tinkering with the deposits interest rates, how can we reduce the real interest 
rates? The opportunity was there. Basic fundamentals of the economy were 
strong — huge buffer stock in foodgrains and huge foreign exchange reserves. 
Instead of Current Account deficit, there is Current Account surplus. Exports 
have started picking up. But, if it is switch-off and switch-on; this year's 18 per 
cent growth reduces to five or six per cent growth next year, it will not help us. 
Whatever growth rate we would like to achieve, it must be sustainable. And, if 
we want to have a sustainable growth, we must take the reality into account. In 
our school days, we used to read two English poems, one composed by Shelly 
and another by Wordsworth. Both of them were Victorian age poets. Shelly's 
skylark always soaring high in the blue sky, described as ethereal minstrel 
pilgrim of the sky but Wordsworth skylark not only flew high in the blue sky, but 
also kept its eyes on the nest, on a tea-top, that means, don't forget the reality. 
Eight per cent GDP growth is absolutely necessary. Creation-of 10 million jobs 
is absolutely necessary. But what disturbs me is this. When Dr. Manmohan 
Singh was the Finance Minister, we had identified certain agro-processed 
industries in order to encourage investment in the agro-processed industries in 
rural areas and build up rural infrastructure by creating cold storages. Look at 
the first Budget, 1989-90. What signal did we send? All the tax concessions 
were withdrawn. . New taxes were imposed. Then two-three years had lapsed. 
Thereafter another announcement had to be made that we would like to build 
up cold storage; we would like to build up infrastructure in the rural areas; 
agro-based industry, agro processed industry is one vital area for the 
development of rural areas and generation of jobs. 
The third point which I am trying to drive at, Mr. Chairman, Sir, is that 
this type of adhoc and causal approach in respect of certain policies must  be 
given  up.     I  have no quarrel with the Plan document.     The 
220 

RAJYA SABHA                 [29 April, 2003] 
problems have been identified properly. Diagnosis is correct and the remedies 
are also suggested correctly. But when the question of the actual 
implementation comes, if medicines are not used in proper manner - there are 
many doctors who are laughing at me and they might be saying why a non-
medical man should talk of a disease -- naturally the medicines would not 
have that impact. We have reached a very crucial stage of our developmental 
planning. 
Lastly, I would like to speak on good governance. I entirely agree 
that that is one of the centrality of our developmental objective. As we have to 
improve the delivery system, we ought to come out of.our mindset; we ought 
to think big; we ought to be competitive. We cannot reverse the process of 
changes which are taking place afl over the world. At the same time, we are to 
provide.good governance, good security and create an environment where 
investors will feel confident. They will not feel shy of. Nothing but good 
governance, continuity of the policies and transparency can create that 
environment where investment would come. 
Still I do believe that higher rate of domestic savings is absolutely 
imperative to have higher rate of investments. Whatever we may think of direct 
foreign investments, whatever we may think of investments from other sources, 
there is no substitute to our own resources and there we must have a stable 
interest regime and that stable interest regime is closely linked with the 
restoration of fiscal balance. We should encourage domestic savings and we 
should encourage savings to be generated in those sectors which are 
achievable. In the terminal years of the Eighth Plan, we achieved 26 per cent 
plus. It came down during the Ninth Plan. Now you are projecting to have 29.6 
per cent. But try to fix that target; reach that target by all means and provide 
the necessary fiscal support regime to achieve these objectives. If we have 
that and with certain other measures -- naturally we cannot discuss all these 
aspects; I have outlined some of the very broad features -- if we can take this 
cautious correct approach with determination, it would be possible to have the 
desired level of growth and our ultimate objective which the Prime Minister has 
very correctly pointed out to create a bold and proud India where everybody 
will have a role to play.   Thank you.

SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN (Assam): Thank you, Madam, for 
giving me an opportunity to say a few words on this subject. The Planning 
Commission under the chairmanship of Prime Minister have made detailed 
plans for Tenth Five-Year Plan period, 2002-2007. The Commission fixed a 
modest target of 8 per cent growth during the period. The. Commission clearly 
states the objectives, and also targets, in different fields of development to our 
country. After carefully considering the promises made by the Commission, I 
am not satisfied with it. Let me take some of them one by one. 
249 

[29 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA  
 
Industry is the most important sector where development should be given 
priority in modern age. This is the sector, which makes the economy vibrant 
for all-round development in our age. But in this field, the Commission has 
given emphasis on completion of partially completed or ongoing projects and 
upgradation of existing capital assets before starting new projects. This 
emphasis laid by the Commission will create greater hardship to the states 
where industrial development is advancing at a snail's pace. North-Eastern 
Region will suffer the most because of some pending projects, and no new 
proposal will come because of this policy. 
Secondly, the Commission gives priority to private sector over public 
sector. It further says that public sector enterprises will be privatised very 
rapidly during this Tenth Five-Year Plan. This is the worst decision for a 
medium developing country like India. Unless the strong public sector thrives 
or this sector is preserved, the country cannot advance. India is not America or 
it is not like developed European countries. This will lead to further imbalance 
in economic development of our country. How can North-Eastern Region, or 
Jammu and Kashmir, or even Orissa and Bihar can advance, unless the public 
sector is there? This policy will further harm the employment sector. Private 
sector is always after its profit. They have no social interest. And employment 
facilities will be less and less after the policy of this privatisation is fully 
implemented. The Government's policy of selling or disinvesting the PSUs will 
lead to further unemployment. According to the Commission', the current 
backlog of unemployed people is 35 million, which is about 9 per cent at 
present, and it is too high. But the Prime Minister promised to bring 
employment for 50 million people, during the Tenth Five-Year Plan. But one 
year has passed without having the promised 10 million jobs. The propaganda 
of giving jobs in unorganised sector is a hoax. What people want? It is not 
temporary jobs; they want jobs of permanent nature.   But it is not done. 
In Assam, 22 lakh are registered unemployed. But no industry is 
being proposed to create employment. The stipulated gas cracker unit may not 
be coming into existence before ten years due to bunglings of Reliance 
Industries Ltd., the ONGC and others. Then, private persons, entrepreneurs or 
companies do not go to Assam for establishing industries due to lack of 
infrastructure, communication and for the wrong-doings of some of the 
extremist forces. The Commission will find it difficult to go to the help of Assam 
or North-Eastern States as they have the policy of disinvesting and selling 
public enterprises, and they have no intention to build new industries 
 
250 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2003] 
in public sector there. So, during the Tenth Five-Year Plan, employment 
potentiality for educated youths in Assam or in any other North-Eastern States 
will come to zero. The Commission says, it will give priority to infrastructure 
building. In this sector also, they want private parties to come in. But they 
themselves visualise that private parties may enter or may not enter in this 
sector, or if they enter, they will enter to build little infrastructure. If this is a 
fact, there will be difficulty, particularly in power and energy sector. In road 
building sector also, though some very good schemes have been announced, 
yet some parts of the country, including the North-East, are suffering, and will 
be suffering. The promises given by the Ministers, from time to time, are not 
fulfilled in the North-East, though there is a very good potential, to connect the 
belt, full of raw material, by good roads and to produce the cheapest hydro-
electric power for the development of the region. But this is not done. No plan 
has been visualised to harness the Brahmaputra river by establishing the 
projects visualised by the Brahmaputra Board. 
Madam, during the Tenth Five Year Plan, many new roads like 
Dhodar Ali could have been made into National Highways in the North East. 
But the Planning Commission did not have any such proposal. 
In the field of agriculture, where 70 per cent of our total population is 
involved, directly or indirectly, the same privatisation policy will affect the 
sector. In the field of irrigation and water management, the policy is yet to 
materialise. The mechanised cultivation cannot be run unless the irrigation 
system is there in every place, in every season of the year. The Tenth Plan is 
also on the same line, as taken by the previous Plans. This will also create 
unequal economfc development in different parts of the country. 
In the field of fertilisers, the whole Eastern Region of our country will 
have to depend either on imports or by bringing fertilisers from other parts of 
the country, as all the public sector fertiliser plants like Sindri, Talcher, (Time-
bell) Durgapur, Barauni, etc., are closed on grounds of loss-making. Who 
made them loss-making? It is obvious that the Government is responsible for 
this. The Planning Commission has no vision to revive these units in the public 
sector. 
Though there is a vision by the Planning Commission, yet it is not up 
to the expectation of the people of new century, or, the new millennium. It may 
create further uneven economic development of the country, which may lead 
to further social dissensions and disruptions.

[29 April. 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Madam, North East is a very neglected region, though some good 
proposals of funding like Nonlapsable Pool are there. Hon. Shri Pranab 
Mukherjee has dealt with this issue. Actually, this Fund is not properly 
administered. So, this region will be further alienated. Due to uneven economic 
development, regional imbalance will also be increasing. So, I urge upon the 
hon. Prime Minister to look into these matters, when he, as the Chairman, will 
review the Tenth Plan. I request the Prime Minister to do some thing for the 
development of the country, as a whole. Thank you. 
SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN (Nominated): Thank you, Madam Deputy-
Chairperson. The Tenth Five Year Pl an is a heavy load of printed paper, 
difficult to carry in the hand, and almost impossible to carry it- in the head. 
There are so many aspects. Madam, to deal with, but I will concentrate on a 
very few. I believe, the Prime Minister's Forewords to the Five Year Plan has 
placed the entire concept of planning in the correct perspective. The message 
is focussed on good governance and implementation and the quote is, "that 
the best policies and programmes can flounder on the rock of poor governance 
and shortcomings in implementation". These are words of wisdom that must 
guide all discussions and guide all national endeavours. Good governance then 
is the single most important factor in ensuring that the objectives of the Tenth 
Plan are achieved. But, I should have thought that the first aspect of good 
governance is spelt out in our Constitution itself, in a chapter now long 
forgotten, Chapter IV, which is the Directive Principles of State Policy. The 
framers of the Tenth Plan have missed the constitutional imperative. Article 37 
says that the principles contained in Chapter IV are fundamental to the 
governance of the country and it is the duty of the State to apply these 
principles in rrmking laws. No one has suggested any amendments to them. 
Everyone today talks of article 21, most of all lawyers, but no one talks of 
article 39 to article 50 which makes life worthwhile. Without these rights, which 
are in these articles, life is just not worth living, it is merely breathing. When we 
nationalised the core industries in the 1970s, we assumed that the PSUs 
would turnaround the country. But they did not. Putting the State into running 
business -was a mistake and it is now realised. Now, when we are reversing 
the process of nationalisation, doesn't matter by what means, which I think is 
necessary, why are we not paying regard to the other provisions in part IV? All 
measures have to be judged on the touchstone of Directive Principles of State 
Policy. That is good governance under our Constitution. And that is the 
touchstone of on which every State of the Union must be judged as to whether 
the State is a State of good governance or it is a State of not good 
252 

RAJYA SABHA                         [29 April, 2003] 
governance. The United Nations have a Human Development Report and they 
publish it every year. Some of the hon. Members mentioned it a moment ago. 
The Planning Commission, I would suggest, should judge every State by 
reference to the principles set out in Chapter IV of the Constitution. 
The next point in governance is people. There are far too many of 
them. Our Constitution was framed when there were only 350 million. Now 
there are more than one billion. The more people there are to govern, the 
more the difficult are the problems of governance. And the Plan tells us that 
changes in age structure of population are such as to lead to a much faster 
growth of population in the working group age and this will lead to a faster 
growth of the labour force. Hence, they suggest that there should be more job 
opportunities. But what is alarming is that with such a high growth as 8 per 
cent, the objective oi providing employment opportunities to addition to labour 
force, according to the planners, "will not be achieved". And the answer given

"In this effort, extensive discussions with Ministries and sector, specialists have 
been undergone and at present the awareness of employment generation is 
very poor while formulating plans, programmes and policies. This applies to 
most of the concerned Ministries and authorities." This is truly frightening. 
What are we going to do before the population stabilises in 2045. There is no 
option, I submit, but for the political parties to educate the people, educate 
them about the need to control population. We must. Otherwise, there will be 
no progress. The Planning Commission is not a political body. It should have

which lag behind in 'family welfare' which is a lovely euphemism, by which we 
all describe family planning which is absolutely imperative, if we as a country 
are to achieve a substantial economic growth and make progress. One last 
thing, Madam, and that is, the Plan document speaks of conceptualising 
governance and it says, "efficient governance requires efficient- institutions." 
But when dealing with the judicial institutions, there io only one sentence and 
that sentence reads, 'there is an urgent need to bring about judicial reforms 
with a view to speeding up the process of delivering justice. Alternatives   to   
the   regular   delivery   mechanism   through   hierarchy   of

alternative courts like family courts, like Lok Adalats, Nyay Panchayats are

what is needed to be done. It is done every time, every year- in the United 
States. The judiciary does not sit in judgment over the Planning Commission. 
The Planning Commission is neither a political nor a legal body. It is an 
advisory body. And, it must be well informed. And, the judiciary, as a judiciary, 
must acquaint the Planning Commission of its need for resources. And that, I 
submit, ought to be something that should be borne in mind for the future.   
Thank you. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE 
DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC ENERGY AND DEPARTMENT OF SPACE (SHRI 
SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): Madam Deputy Chairperson, the Government 
is very happy that this august House has taken up the discussion on the Tenth 
Five Year Plan. I wish to express my gratitude and thanks to the hon. 
Members who have suggested various steps to be taken in order to make this 
Plan a success. Indeed, I think, the speech of Shri Pranab Mukherjee is one of 
the finest pieces of constructive criticism that I have ever heard. In fact, he has 
thoroughly studied the Plan and also suggested remedial measures that 
should be taken. Madam, we believe that the national   Five   Year .Plans   can   
be   successful   only   when   there   is   an 
254 

RAJYA SABHA                [29 April. 2003] 
understanding of the objectives, strategies and the implementation 
methodologies of the Plan at all levels. Such an understanding is possible only 
when there is a thorough discussion and debate so that all the doubts and 
differences are articulated and addressed. While approving the Approach 
Paper to the Tenth Five Year Plan, the NDC had mandated a set of objectives 
and targets which were essential to enable us to focus on an accelerated 
growth. No Plan, however, can be successful without a thorough discussion. 
Although, the Plan document goes through various stages, it is considered and 
approved by the Planning Commission, by the Cabinet and then by the 
National Development Council. But, still, this is not a substitute for the 
discussions which we have here in this House. What is required is a broad-
based consensus and I hope and believe that we shall be able to achieve that. 
And, today's discussion is pointed in that direction. This Plan has a unique 
feature, in the sense, the various States were taken into confidence. The 
participation of various States, in a larger scale, is very much there and they 
were consulted at every stage, unlike the previous ones when they were 
consulted at the stage of the meetings of the National Development Council, 
or, at the level of the Working Groups consisting of officials. Madam, it is clear 
from the discussion that there are still some apprehensions and 
misapprehensions. 
The first one is with regard to the growth rate. Now, there can be a 
target and a projection. A projection can be achieved in a stage where there is 
"business as usual" scenario. But, 'target' is something visionary. We seek to 
achieve something which we think is possible for us. We have to stretch our 
limits so that we achieve that target. It would have been possible for this 
Government to have a lower growth rate and achieve that. But, we have 
targeted something more; and, it will be our endeavour, at the end of the day, 
to see that this target is reached. Fortunately, none of the Members has said 
that that it cannot be achieved. It may be difficult. And, certainly the endeavour 
of the Government will be to reach this target. Madam, various experts were 
consulted and stakeholders were also consulted. Their suggestion was that 
various reform policies and procedures would have to be adopted. I also wish 
to record that the States were, in fact, of the 1 opinion that there should be a 
target on the higher side. And, each one of them had suggested their own 
growth rate. In this vast country, the different States have different growth 
rates. All these have been taken into consideration to arrive at the figure of 
eight per cent growth rate. What I could follow from the discussion is that the 
main problem is with regard to implementation.    Now, we have taken two 
major measures with 
255 

[29 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
regard to implementation. One is that the National Development Ccurttil has 
directed the constitution of four Empowered Sub-Committee*-;., consisting of 
the Central Ministers and the State Chief Ministers to deviso and oversee the 
implementation of the four  most contentious area s --removing barriers among 
inter-State trade, creating an investor-friendly climate, governance reforms, 
and the empowerment of the panchayati raj institutions. Madam, the four 
committees have been constituted, and apart from that the Government has a 
priority agenda, and the entire implementation procedure will be overseen and 
monitored by a Cabinet Committee. In this context, I would like to quote what 
the Prime Minister had said. He said, "The question is not whether we can 
grow faster, but, whether we can afford not to...." This country has tremendous 
potential and it will be our endeavour, at the end of the day, to see that this 
potential, keeping that in mind, we could achieve the target. 
Another aspect of the Plan document is that it does not only focus on 
growth, its main objective is to improve the quality of life of our people. For this 
purpose, there are certain monitorable targets, which I would like to place 
before this House. These are: reduction of the poverty ratio by five points; 
providing gainful and high quality employment; all children in school by 2003; 
all children to complete five year of schooling by 2007; reduction in gender gaps 
in literacy and wage rates; reduction in the growth rate of population; increase 
in the literacy rate to 75 per cent; reduction in infant mortality rate to forty-five 
per one thousand live births; reduction in maternal mortality rate to two per one 
thousand live births; increase in forest and tree cover to 25 per cent; all 
villages to have sustained access to potable drinking water; and, cleaning all 
major polluted rivers. Then, Madam, on the employment front, there are 
various schemes under which it is the intention of the Government to create 
employment opportunities. It is not that everybody will be getting a Central 
Government job, but, then, an opportunity will be there, even for self-
employment. And the emphasis, Madam, will be that employment generated 
will be largely shown in the private sector and specially, as self-employment. 
Then, Madam, savings and investment is another sector, which 
various Members have addressed. And the real issue is not whether the 
projected improvement in Government savings, which is, in fact, the major 
source of additional savings for the Plan, can be realised. Improving 
Government finances necessarily involves hard decisions since it means either 
higher tax collections, or, reductions in expenditure, or both; none of 
256 

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2003] 
which is politically popular. This is also one point which Shri Pranab Mukherjee 
had highlighted. Now, in fact, we have to take steps to increase the collection 
of taxes and also^to reduce the Government expenditure. These are two major 
spheres where this is attempted. 
Now, there were certain arguments advanced with regard to the 
resistance to the subsidies being withdrawn. But, Madam, there are certain 
spheres where there are needless exemptions being given, which also, we 
think, ought to be tightened so that some money may be available. And, in 
fact, some of the States have shown the way by withdrawing the subsidies; 
power subsidies, for instance. And, it is the intention of this Government also 
to follow suit in some spheres where it is possible. 
Then, Madam, about the question of disinvestment, a lot of debate 
has taken place on this aspect, and I would say that it is not stripping of 
assets, but a switching of assets because the money that is available will be 
utilized in another sphere. And it is not the intention of this Government, really, 
to strip the assets of the Government, but to utilize the proceeds, which will be 
available for development purposes. 
Then, Madam, on the question of FDI, if I am permitted, I would like 
to quote from the Tenth Plan Document itself. It says, "An investor friendly 
climate needs to be created in the country for all investments, and not just for 
foreign investors. Indeed, it is submitted that if the investment climate, in 
general, is improved, no exclusive measures may be needed to attract foreign 
investors." 
Then, Madam, special emphasis has been given to rural 
development under this Plan and various schemes have been suggested, 
because 70 per cent people of our country lives in villages, and they depend 
on agriculture, and that sphere ought to be, certainly, developed in the interest 
of our economy. Then, Madam, the power sector also requires more 
generation of electricity, and also the saving of electricity, because a large 
amount of electricity so generated is stolen; that has to be stopped. 
Then, in the Information Technology sector also, there is a great 
scope and the Government is, certainly, conscious of that; and is laying 
special emphasis on that. 
So far as the infrastructure is concerned, the National Highway 
Development Project, which consists of the Golden Quadrilateral roads, and 
the North-South, East-West corridors. These, if and when completed, would

[29 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
also be a great achievement and these also provide a great scope for 
employment in course of execution of these projects. Then, Pradhan Mantri 
Gram Sadak Yojana, I think, is one of the best projects that has been 
undertaken. As regards village connectivity, we have seen that in the villages 
there are no roads at all, and this Project, if implemented, will provide a great 
source of income, and the connectivity will enable the villagers to have access 
to the urban areas. 
Madam, there are other points which were made by the hon. 
Members. I will just take one or two points. Shri Pranab Mukherjee, in fact, as I 
said, in his constructive criticism, has made certain suggestions which will, 
certainly, be borne in mind. One of the points which he emphasised was that 
proper implementation was required. He also emphasised on good 
governance. Madam, the Government is conscious of the fact, about good 
governance. With regard to domestic savings, that also has been taken care of 
in the Plan document. These are really important points which will, certainly, 
be looked after. In fact, they are there in the Plan document itself. 
Then, hon. Members have suggested the improvement of cottage 
industries and village industries. That, certainly, has also been taken care of in 
the Plan document, and the Government is conscious of this fact. 
Then, in the end, Mr. Nariman, of course, emphasised the question of 
good governance. He referred to Chapter IV of the Constitution, relating to 
Directive Principles. Gf course, he has taken a legalistic view of the matter, but 
the root of the entire good governance lies in the Constitution itself, and we are 
conscious of that fact. 
Madam, another aspect which was emphasised by the Members was 
the population control. We are all consious of that, but, unfortunately, we have 
not been able to achieve great success in that sphere. For that purpose, I 
think, education is a must. In this Plan document, there is Sarva Siksha 
Abhiyan which has been mentioned.   There are other Schemes also. 
With regard to employment also, various schemes have been 
provided like the Swaran Jayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana and the Sampoorna 
Grameen Rojgar Yojana. These are the schemes which have been taken into 
consideration to provide greater employment opportunities.

RAJYA SABHA [29 April, 2003] 
Madam, taking an overall view of the matter, I respectfully submit, as 
has been said by various Members also, that this Plan document does take 
into consideration the various problems which the country is facing and the

day, we shall be able to achieve success and implement the provisions of the 
Plan.   With these words, Madam, I conclude. Thank you.
